readerTitle: What craigslist really took from newspapers
caseNote: 실제 기업 (craigslist, 미국 지역 신문) + 실제 연구 (Seamans & Zhu, 2014) + 가상 적용 (배관 업체, 호텔)
insight: 어떤 수익원이 사업의 나머지를 먹여 살리는지 알면, 경쟁자가 어디부터 공격할지 보인다.
misconception: 신문은 무료 사이트에 광고 몇 개를 뺏겼을 뿐이다. 가격만 맞추면 지킬 수 있다.

sources.text: craigslist, About / Factsheet 페이지 (1995년 이메일 리스트로 시작, 유료 카테고리, 배너 광고 없음)
Seamans, R. & Zhu, F. (2014). Responses to Entry in Multi-Sided Markets: The Impact of Craigslist on Local Newspapers. Management Science.
Pew Research Center, Newspapers Fact Sheet / Newspaper Association of America 광고 매출 자료 (분류광고 매출 추이)
배관 업체와 호텔 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: craigslist가 1995년 샌프란시스코 행사 이메일 리스트로 시작해 웹사이트가 되었고 2000년대에 여러 도시로 확장했다는 내용을 craigslist 공식 자료로 확인하세요.
유료 카테고리: 오랫동안 일부 도시의 구인 광고와 뉴욕의 일부 중개인 임대 매물 등 소수 카테고리만 유료였습니다. 최근에는 유료 카테고리가 늘었으므로 카드에 "for most of its history"로 적었습니다. 게시 전 현재 요금 페이지를 확인하세요.
"작은 팀", "배너 광고 없음"은 널리 보도된 내용이나 직원 수는 시기별로 다르므로 숫자를 쓰지 않았습니다.
미국 신문 분류광고 매출이 2000년 무렵 정점을 찍고 이후 10년간 급감했다는 내용을 NAA/Pew 자료로 확인하세요. 분류광고가 신문 매출의 '큰 몫'이었다는 표현도 수치 없이 정성적으로만 썼습니다.
Seamans & Zhu(2014)의 결과 중 'craigslist 진출 지역 신문이 분류광고 가격을 낮추고 구독료를 올렸다'는 방향만 적었습니다. 구체적 % 수치는 쓰지 않았으니 원문에서 방향을 다시 확인하세요.

cards.eyebrow: Ways to make money · Company story
cards.title: What craigslist really took from newspapers
body: For decades, a big share of a US local newspaper's money came from tiny ads at the back: a used car, a room for rent, a restaurant hiring a cook.
Then a plain-looking website started taking the same ads, mostly for free. The website hardly changed. The newspapers changed a lot.

image.label: A thick newspaper whose back pages turn into a simple web list
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 두꺼운 신문의 뒷부분 분류광고 면이 한 장씩 날아가며 단순한 텍스트 목록 화면으로 바뀌는 장면. 실제 신문 제호나 craigslist 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A free rival comes for your classifieds.
body: It's around 2000. You publish a city newspaper. Classified ads are one of your biggest sources of income, and that money helps pay your reporters.
A website now lets people post the same ads for free, and it's growing fast in your city. What's your move?

options.text: Wait it out. Readers trust the paper, and serious sellers will stay
options.feedback: You keep today's income for a while. But sellers go where buyers are, and once buyers move online, loyalty to the paper won't hold the ads.

options.text: Cut classified prices to keep advertisers
options.feedback: It may slow the exit, but every cut shrinks the money that pays your newsroom. You're fighting on price with a rival that has no newsroom to pay for.

options.text: Assume classified money will shrink, and start building other ways to pay for the newsroom
options.feedback: It's slow and painful, and it stops defending the old income. But it faces the real problem: the ads paid for something the rival never had to fund.

cards.title: An email list became a free classifieds site.
body: Craig Newmark started craigslist in 1995 as an email list of events in San Francisco. It became a website and, through the 2000s, spread to cities across the US and beyond.

For most of its history, most posts were free. It charged only in a few categories, such as job ads in some cities and certain apartment listings in New York. It ran with a **small team** and no banner ads.

cards.title: The back pages emptied out.
body: US newspaper classified revenue peaked around 2000, then fell steeply over the next decade. Craigslist wasn't the only cause. Job sites, property sites and search engines took ads too.
Researchers Robert Seamans and Feng Zhu studied local papers. Where craigslist arrived, papers **charged less for classified ads** and raised subscription prices to make up some of the gap.

image.label: Newspaper classified pages shrinking over the years
image.brief: 왼쪽부터 오른쪽으로 신문 뭉치 다섯 개가 점점 얇아지는 일러스트. 연도 라벨이나 수치는 넣지 않음. 마지막 신문 옆에 "Classifieds" 라벨의 빈 페이지.

cards.title: Cross-subsidy
body: A **cross-subsidy** is when one part of a business earns more than it costs, so another part can be cheaper or exist at all.

Classified ads were cheap to run and earned well. That money helped pay for reporters, editors, printing and delivery. Craigslist had none of those costs, so it could charge nothing for most ads and still run.
A rival that offers only your profitable piece doesn't carry your other costs.

image.label: Classified ad money flowing to a newsroom, printing press and delivery truck
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 왼쪽 "Classified ads" 상자에서 화살표가 "Reporters", "Printing", "Delivery"로 갈라져 흐름. 오른쪽에는 "Free listings site" 상자가 단독으로 있고 화살표는 "Servers, small team" 하나뿐.

cards.softwareNote: Many software companies use one profitable product to fund free tiers or newer products. If a focused rival offers just the profitable product for less, the whole arrangement is at risk.

cards.title: It happens to a plumber too.
body: A plumbing firm charges well for emergency call-outs. That margin keeps its yearly check-up plan cheap, which keeps customers loyal.
Then an app starts sending independent plumbers to emergencies for less. They run no check-up plans, so they don't need the extra margin. The firm's most profitable work is now its most exposed.
The question to ask: **which part pays for the rest**, and who could sell just that part?

cards.title: Cross-subsidies aren't a mistake.
body: Most businesses have them. A café's coffee may carry its food. A bundle can serve customers better than separate parts.

The risk appears when the paying part is easy to split off and sell alone. And one cheap rival is rarely the whole story. Newspapers also lost readers' time and display ads to the wider internet. Blaming a single rival can hide the bigger shift.

cards.title: Now it's a hotel.
body: Your hotel's event hall is booked most weekends for weddings and conferences. Its profit helps you keep room rates low.
A new event venue opens nearby with no hotel to run, and it charges far less for its hall. What do you do?

options.text: Match its hall price to keep the bookings
options.feedback: You keep the calendar full, but the profit that kept room rates low disappears. You're in a price fight with a rival that carries fewer costs.

options.text: Focus on events that need rooms, like weddings with out-of-town guests, and set room prices as if hall profit will shrink
options.feedback: You give up some local events, but you compete where your hotel adds value the rival can't match, and you stop leaning on margin that's under attack.

options.text: Add free extras to the hall package to justify the price
options.feedback: It may hold some bookings for a while. But extras cost money, and they don't give guests who need no rooms a reason to pay more.

cards.title: Know which sale pays for the rest.
body: The revenue stream that funds the rest of your business is the one a focused rival will target first. Craigslist didn't need to beat newspapers at news. It only needed the ads.
**Try it today:** list your three most profitable products or services. For each, write what it helps pay for, and who could sell just that piece for less.
